episodes.180701: A few thunderstorms became severe across Laramie and Goshen Counties 15 July.

episodes.180758: Higher low-level moisture on July 13th and a backdoor cold front replenishing this moisture for July 14th and 15th combined with robust upper level wind shear produced three days of severe weather across eastern NM. Severe weather impacts were limited to northeastern NM on the 13th and 14th, becoming more widespread across northeastern and east-central NM on the 15th. There were a few thunderstorm wind gusts measured in the vicinity of the White Sands Missile Range on the 13th and 14th, likely from dry microbursts as the exception for the 13th and 14th. More substantial reports of damage and large hail occurred on the 15th ranging from broken skylights, flooding, accumulated hail, and a tornado. Thankfully, there were no reports of injuries or casualties.
episodes.180766: A trough of low pressure was situated from Buckingham County, VA southeast through Alleghany County, NC during the evening of the 15th, while a cold front was advancing eastward across the mountains.  A wave of low pressure passing along the front over western North Carolina served to increase  low level winds into the 20 kt-25 kt range from the south, tapping into deep moisture.  By 8 pm EDT, precipitable water values across Campbell and Appomattox Counties had risen as high as 2.1 inches, which is around 2 standard deviations above normal for mid-July for central Virginia per NWS gridded climatology estimates.  Instability was also observed to be extremely high, with surface-based CAPE values in the 2,500 to 3,000 J/Kg range.  By 10 pm EDT, storms that had made steady progress southeast across Bedford County were beginning to stall along the surface trough stretching across Campbell and Appomattox Counties.  Steady flow of moisture from the south continued to feed into the line of storms, with cells beginning to train over the same locations. High instability continue to support rainfall rates within the stronger cells of 4+ inches per hour.  By 11 pm EDT, CREST Unit Streamflows were beginning to exceed 600 cfs per mi^2 across the southern portion of the City of Lynchburg into northern Campbell County, persisting as such through 1 am EDT on the 16th, when heavy rain exited the area.  FLASH 3-hour Average Recurrence Intervals were observed approaching a 200-year rainfall event just north of the Town of Rustburg.  This resulted in considerable flooding across Campbell county and Lynchburg.
episodes.180770: An isolated severe thunderstorm produced wind damage.
episodes.180823: Thunderstorms brought locally heavy rain to northern New Jersey from the late afternoon into the evening of July 14.  Rainfall totals were as high as 3 to around 7 inches.
episodes.180824: Thunderstorms brought locally heavy rain to the Lehigh Valley and the Pocono Region of eastern Pennsylvania from the late afternoon into the evening of July 14.  Rainfall totals were as high as 3 to around 6 inches.
episodes.180828: Thunderstorms brought locally heavy rain to parts of central New Jersey from the late afternoon into the evening of July 15.  Rainfall totals were as high as 3 to 5 inches.
episodes.180829: Thunderstorms brought locally heavy rain to parts of eastern Pennsylvania from the late afternoon into the evening of July 15.  Rainfall totals were as high as 3 to 6 inches.  Catastrophic flash flooding occurred in Upper Makefield Township in Bucks County, where several lives were lost.
episodes.181060: A stationary front extended across the northern sections of Southwest Arkansas on July 15th, as a weak upper level disturbance rounded the upper ridge in place over the Southern Plains near the front. A hot and very humid air mass in place near the front contributed to very strong instability, as large scale forcing increased in advance of this disturbance. Thus, scattered severe thunderstorms developed along the front, and tracked southeast from Northern Nevada into Ouachita and Northern Union Counties, with damaging winds downing trees and power lines across Northern Union County in the Norphlet community before exiting the area into Ashley County by late afternoon.
episodes.181220: Showers and thunderstorms developed in West Virginia on the afternoons of July 13th through 15th in the midst of weak disturbances passing through the area.  Strong wind gusts accompanying storms resulted in multiple downed trees across the state. Flash flooding also blocked sections of a road in Raleigh County on the 13th while another isolated instance of flash flooding occurred on the 15th in Clay County. Storms tapered down with the loss of daytime heating after sunset each evening.
episodes.181425: An isolated severe thunderstorm drifted very slowly southward, then became stationary in the vicinity of Mcleansboro. Isolated wind damage was followed by flash flooding once the storm stopped moving. The storm formed ahead of a cold front that trailed southwest across central Missouri from a low pressure center over the Great Lakes.
episodes.181535: Daytime heating helped the environment become unstable enough for severe thunderstorms that were kicked off by a frontal system. The storms developed east of I-81 in Central New York and produced damaging wind gusts and large hail.
episodes.181602: A upper level disturbance along with building instability led to a cluster of showers and thunderstorms riding east along the south shore of Lake Ontario late in the afternoon. These storms caused gusty winds to 35 knots on Lake Ontario.
episodes.181649: A cluster of thunderstorms moved over southern portions of Lake Michigan and produced stronger winds.
episodes.181656: A weak surface trough and upper level disturbance led to scattered thunderstorms across southern WI. One storm become severe causing tree damage.
episodes.181771: Scattered afternoon thunderstorms produce isolated reports of damaging winds across portions of northeast Tennessee. An isolated flash flood also occurred.
episodes.181780: On the morning of July 15th, a line of showers and embedded thunderstorms developed along a low level disturbance passing through eastern Kentucky. While most of the activity contributed to no storm damage, there was one instance of a downed tree in Greenup County due to a strong gust of wind accompanying the passing storm.
episodes.181781: Showers and thunderstorms developed on the afternoon of July 15th along a low level disturbance crossing through the Ohio Valley. Embedded within this cluster of activity, a few storms reached strong to severe levels, and resulted in damaging wind gusts. As one of those storms passed through Lawrence County, the strong wind gusts resulted in downed trees in Chesapeake and South Point.
episodes.181886: The remnants of a frontal boundary from the previous day ignited additional widely scattered thunderstorms during the early evening hours. Most of the wind damage was localized over southern Maryland, where spotty large hail was also reported.
episodes.181939: A cold front slowed as it approached the Appalachian Mountains, intersecting a hot, humid, and unstable airmass. This resulted in scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms, several of which produced gale- to storm-force winds near the area waterways.
episodes.182103: A hot and humid airmass was in place across central Illinois as a cold front approached from the northwest. Several thunderstorm clusters developed over the course of the evening, and these produced scattered wind damage and one instance of severe hail.
episodes.182159: As a cold front approached from the west throughout the day, showers and storms were on tap for portions of eastern Kentucky. While these storms did not become severe or cause much impact from the winds or hail, they did put down some heavy rains. This led to 2 isolated reports of flooding in both Martin and Knott counties due to streams running high.
episodes.182172: A long-track mesoscale convective system (MCS) tracked from southern Nebraska into the Ozarks during daytime hours on the 14th. The southwestern portion of this system clipped the far northeast forecast area (Kay County) and produced a report of wind damage near Ponca City. Further west, scattered supercell thunderstorms developed by the evening hours and produced reports of large hail near the community of Woodward.
episodes.182251: On the evening of July 15th isolated thunderstorms developed across southern New Hampshire.  Storm movement mitigated flash flooding across the state, except for the city of Manchester where multiple storms traveled directly over the city on the evening of July 15th.  Up to 2��� fell in an hour over the urban city area.  The intense rainfall rates lead to rapid run-off and caused localized urban street flooding with water due to run-off entering some building structures.  Lighter showers passed across the area later in the evening before rain ended.||On July 16th a more widespread area of rain impacted most of the state.  Rain showers began to develop around daybreak on July 16th and quickly became more widespread during the morning hours.  Light to moderate rainfall became widespread across the state with embedded bands of heavy rain.  Locally heavy rainfall continued straight through the morning hours into early afternoon on the 16th before rainfall intensity and coverage began to decrease.  Central and Southern New Hampshire received the heaviest rainfall through the day, with less rainfall across the Connecticut River Valley and the Seacoast.  Rainfall amounts of 2+��� were widespread across Central New Hampshire with two corridors of locally heavier rain in this area.  One corridor of heavy rain was from eastern Cheshire County through northwest Hillsborough County and into Central Merrimack County.  Observed reports of 3+��� of rain occurred in this region with one localized report of 4+���.  The heavy rain caused isolated areas of flooded roads along with wash-outs in Antrim where a localized area of heavy rain occurred.  The second corridor of heavy rain across the state was the most significant for the event.  This corridor of rain ran from the Massachusetts border around Nashua all the way to the Maine border in southern Carroll County.  There were numerous reports of 3+��� of rain with localized areas receiving over 4��� of rainfall by early afternoon.  The majority of this rainfall fell in a 3 to 4 hour window in the late morning hours.  The heavy rainfall rates and saturated grounds led to rapid run-off of small streams and creeks which led to flash flooding.  Flash flooding was considerable in the Barnstead, Alton and Wolfeboro region where numerous roads were closed due to severe flooding and wash-outs.  Additional urban flash flooding also occurred in the Manchester area due to flooded roads.  Minor property flooding was also reported on numerous lakefronts across the region due to very high lake levels after this rain event.   ||Localized river flooding also occurred in response to the July 15-16th rainfall with river flooding beginning on July 16th and lasting through the 18th, with river crests occurring on July 17th.  The Warner River touched minor flood stage with no significant impacts.  The Suncook River crested at 3.53ft above flood stage on July 17th.  This led to flooding of campgrounds along the river that caused the evacuation of at least one located in the floodplain. All rivers dropped below flood stage on July 18th.||In addition to the flooding, the environment supported a conditional threat for severe weather as the abundant low level moisture and strong low level jet caused significant low level shear.  This caused for numerous storms to have rotation with them that triggered tornado warnings but no tornadoes were confirmed.  There was however some localized tree damage with the associated thunderstorms across Southern New Hampshire.
episodes.182339: Scattered thunderstorms moved through the area during the morning hours in association with an upper level low pressure system.
episodes.182462: Thunderstorms developed, with some becoming severe, as a wave of low pressure passing along the front over western North Carolina served to increase 925 mb and 850 mb winds into the 20 kt-25 kt range from the south, tapping into deep moisture over the eastern Carolinas. By 8 pm EDT, precipitable water values across northwest North Carolina had risen as high as 2.1 inches, which is around 2 standard deviations above normal for mid-July per NWS gridded climatology estimates. Instability was also observed to be extremely high, with surface-based CAPE values in the 2,500 to 3,000 J/Kg range.  In Alleghany County, a thunderstorm produced over 7 inches of rain within a 6-hour period across the headwaters of Glade Creek, with prolonged rainfall rates at 3 inches per hour.  MRMS FLASH CREST Unit Streamflows registered between 600 and 800 cfs per mi^2 due to this rainfall, while 3-hour QPE/FFG indicated that the rainfall was between 2.25 and 2.5 times of the 3-hour flash flood guidance.
episodes.182465: A weak front coupled with an upper level disturbance and afternoon heating allowed for storms to develop, some being severe and producing a few areas of wind damage.
episodes.182515: Scattered thunderstorms, some with torrential rainfall affected portions of Essex County on July 14. Two to locally five inches of rain fell in a some areas, leading to a few reports of flash flooding and road washouts.
episodes.182518: Scattered thunderstorms, some with torrential rainfall affected scattered areas across Vermont on July 14. Two to locally four inches of rain fell in a some areas, leading to a few reports of flash flooding and road washouts.
episodes.182775: A left split supercell produced 1-inch hail just west of Lincoln in the early evening.
episodes.182881: An outbreak of multicell clusters and supercells developed across Southeast Michigan on the afternoon of July 14, 2023. These storms produced areas of wind damage, large hail to golf ball size, heavy rain, and an EF0 tornado in Sanilac County before moving eastward into Canada and the lakes during the evening. Numerous trees were downed across the region, and in the Thumb there were several reports of destroyed corn and wheat fields as well as several homes with damage to siding due to wind-blown hail.
episodes.182992: A typical summer pattern persisted with scattered thunderstorms across the area with a few reports of severe weather.
episodes.182998: A typical summer pattern persisted with scattered thunderstorms across the area with a few reports of severe weather.  In addition, weak steering flow resulted in some slow moving storms with reports of flash flooding, particularly in Jackson and Walton counties.
episodes.183003: A typical summer pattern persisted with scattered thunderstorms across the area with a few reports of severe weather.

episodes.183113: Several clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms moved southeast across portions of northwestern Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 14th. The strongest storms produced damaging wind, a brief tornado, and flash flooding in Sebastian County.||Additional thunderstorms intensified and became well-organized over Kansas during the day as they moved southeast across the state. These thunderstorms formed a nearly solid line of strong to severe thunderstorms that moved across northwestern Arkansas during the evening. The strongest storms produced damaging wind.
episodes.183128: A few strong to marginally severe afternoon and evening thunderstorms developed along I-20, east of Atlanta. Storms caused localized wind damage.
episodes.183154: A strong thunderstorm produced a 43-mph wind gust at the Coast Guard Station in Marquette on the early morning of the 15th.
episodes.183346: Perhaps the most impactful severe weather in July spread from northwest into central and southeast sections of the state on the 14th/15th. Two to more than three inches of rain fell from Fort Smith (Sebastian County) to Waldron (Scott County) and Mena (Polk County). ||Little Rock National Airport (Pulaski County) had a gust of 58 mph. A tree fell on a camping vehicle at Diamond City (Boone County), and a barn was overturned near Whiteville (Baxter County). Trees were toppled near Fairview (Ouachita County).||There were spotty instances of hail/damaging wind across the northern and central counties on the 17th/18th.
episodes.183438: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms ahead and along a cold frontal boundary resulted in widespread downed trees and wires and a few reports of flooding across eastern New York during the afternoon and evening hours of July 13, 2023. One injury was reported as a tree fell onto an occupied vehicle. Thousands were left without power across the Capital Region.||Additional isolated to scattered thunderstorms developed during the evening and early overnight hours on July 14-15, 2023 producing additional reports of hail, wind damage and flooding.
episodes.183507: Scattered strong to marginally severe storms were seen throughout the area from mid afternoon through the evening. Storms produced damaging winds across parts of western Illinois.
episodes.183533: Storms developed over eastern Oklahoma and southeast Kansas during the evening of the 13th and moved along the Missouri and Arkansas border during the early morning of the 14th. The strongest storms produced up to ping-pong ball sized hail over Oregon County. Rainfall accumulations ranged from one to two inches near the Missouri and Arkansas Border.  A second round of storms developed over central Nebraska during the morning of the 14th and moved southeastward across eastern Kansas and into the  Missouri Ozarks through the evening of the 14th. These storms produced a swath of wind gusts over 60 mph from Fort Scott, Kansas to Branson, and led to widespread tree and powerline damage. Rainfall amounts averaged between one-half inch and one inch along and west of a line from Nevada to Gainesville.
episodes.183778: A severe thunderstorm in Larimer County produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter near Wellington.  In addition, a strong storm produced nickel size hail in Douglas County.
episodes.183913: A brief breakdown of the persistent upper ridge due to a disturbance moving southeast through New Mexico brought isolated severe thunderstorms to Grant and Otero counties with hail and gusty winds.
episodes.183970: Several thunderstorm clusters developed during the afternoon and evening along a surface trough across the western Carolinas. One of the embedded cells produced brief damaging wind gusts in Greenwood County.
episodes.183978: A few shortwaves moved through the area, with showers and thunderstorms developing in multiple rounds. Severe thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts in parts of New Jersey.
episodes.183986: A weak frontal boundary approached from the west, which resulted in scattered showers and thunderstorms developing. A few storms became severe, producing damaging wind gusts.
episodes.183988: A weak frontal boundary approached from the west, which resulted in scattered showers and thunderstorms developing. A few storms became severe, producing damaging wind gusts.
episodes.184108: A 500 MB trough and a surface cold front helped trigger heavy rains over and near southwestern Virginia.
episodes.184129: The continuations of hail, wind, and tornadoes continues through mid-July as northwesterly upper level flow develops once again over southern Colorado. Anomalous amounts of low level moisture remain over the region due to record breaking precipitation in June and an active early July. Enhanced wind shear due from the upper level northwesterly flow created an environment conducive to severe thunderstorms.
episodes.184205: During the evening of July 14, severe thunderstorms brought damaging winds to northern Illinois as well as one EF-0 tornado that tracked from Warrenville to Glen Ellyn.
episodes.184344: Isolated storms developed in an area where dewpoints in the low to mid 70s pooled. There was some weak surface convergence, ML CAPEs over 2000 J/kg, and steep low-level lapse rates, so there were some localized damaging microbursts with the severe storms. An area of storms over northern St. Clair County in Illinois produced up to 5 inches of rain in about a two hour period with some reports of flash flooding.
episodes.184345: Isolated storms developed in an area where dewpoints in the low to mid 70s pooled. An area of storms over northern St. Clair County in Illinois produced up to 5 inches of rain in about a two hour period with some reports of flash flooding.
episodes.184362: Isolated thunderstorm associated with a surface trough of low pressure produced gusty winds across portions of the James River.
episodes.184364: Scattered thunderstorms associated with a surface trough of low pressure produced heavy rain which caused flash flooding across portions of central Virginia.
episodes.184539: A very subtle surface trough axis moved generally eastward over western Lake Erie and vicinity during the evening of July 14th as a high pressure ridge exited eastward. Isolated clusters of multicell showers and thunderstorms associated with low-level convergence along the surface trough axis moved east-southeastward over western Lake Erie and northwest OH. A couple of gale-force peak convective wind gusts accompanied these cells along the northwest OH shore as the showers and storms encountered moderate MUCAPE and strong effective bulk shear.
episodes.184544: A weak surface low wobbled east-southeastward from southern Lake Michigan to northeastern IN during the late morning through early evening of July 15th. Simultaneously, the trailing cold front drifted eastward across much of IN as the low's accompanying warm front advanced northeastward from the Middle OH Valley to northern OH. A marginal supercell embedded in a cluster of showers and thunderstorms produced minor straight-line convective wind damage in Ghent as the showers and storms persisted northeastward along the warm front and encountered moderate effective bulk shear and MUCAPE, respectively.
episodes.185221: Scattered late afternoon storms produced damaging winds across southeast Arkansas.
episodes.186183: Isolated thunderstorms brought small hail and gusty winds to parts of northwest Indiana during the afternoon of the 15th. While these storms were believed to be sub-severe, one large tree was blown over in Chesterton.
episodes.186200: A swath of thunderstorms moved over southern Lake Michigan during the late evening of the 14th bringing strong winds and heavy rain to the area.

Catastrophic flash flooding occurred in Upper Makefield Township, resulting in the loss of seven lives.  A reliable rain gauge located within the township indicated that 4.64 inches of rain fell during the event which lasted less than 2 hours.  Widespread roadway flooding occurred with many roads becoming impassable.  Numerous water rescues took place in the township.  The worst of the flooding occurred along Hough's Creek.  The creek rose rapidly and the rushing water carried away many vehicles, most along Taylorsville Road which parallels the Delaware Canal.  Eleven vehicles were reported to have been swept into the creek.  Eight individual were rescued from their vehicle and two from the creek.  Unfortunately, seven people perished either while trapped in their vehicle or while attempting to escape the flood waters.||The Taylorsville Road Bridge over Hough's Creek was structurally compromised.  PA Route 532 between Stonebridge Crossing Road and Wrightstown Road was damaged severely by the raging flood waters from Hough's Creek.
